chapters.title: The Door on Its Rail
chapters.text: Ciro Avellan reached the southern field on the first morning of the year, when only the duty crew was there. Lucia Ferro met the bus with a promise already kept: a bunk by the window, aired and made. Hector Mendaro came down from the tower with three coffees and an apology for the fourth. Inside the hangar Ines Carvalho was writing in a green cloth-bound ledger that was plainly not the station logbook. Ciro wanted to be useful before anyone asked, so he put his shoulder to the big door. One wheel jumped its rail and the bottom edge folded with a sound like a dropped tray. Lucia said everyone did that once. Ines looked up, then back at her page, and left the pencil where he could reach it. The commander's car was due at ten.

options.label: Tell Ines how the door came off its rail.
options.reply: Ines writes the morning into her ledger with Ciro's name beside it; Lucia laughs, then admits she would have helped him hide it.

options.label: Help Lucia lever it back before ten.
options.reply: A shim from Lucia's pocket puts the wheel back on its rail, and Hector keeps the commander talking at the gate a minute longer than necessary.

chapters.title: A Tag on a String
chapters.text: The field's hydraulic test stand had failed in March for want of a seal nobody had ordered; the seal money had gone on paint before an inspection. Ines's ledger said so in two plain lines. Hector solved the rest with one telephone call across the runway. Faria, foreman of the civil airport's workshop, sent his own stand over on a trailer with a brown cardboard tag tied to the handle: back by Friday. Faria's managers did not know they had lent anything, and the commander preferred that the budget review never learn the field had borrowed. Lucia had promised Faria his Friday and promised Ciro a Saturday check that needed the stand. Ciro offered to work all night so that both promises could be kept. Ines asked a smaller question: where would the loan be written, and under whose name?

options.label: Write the loan into the station book, Faria's name and all.
options.reply: Hector telephones Faria before the page goes anywhere, and the foreman's thanks come back cooler than his stand.

options.label: Keep the loan a handshake between Hector and Faria.
options.reply: Faria keeps his stand and his managers' good opinion; Ines notes the loan in her ledger, where no budget review will ever look.

chapters.title: Two Miles North
chapters.text: The weak coast set in Hector's tower was the only receiver at the field that could hear small boats after dark. At nine it carried Amaro Reis, skipper of the Constancia, with a dead engine and a southerly wind pushing him toward the reef. Hector relayed the position to the coast station and stayed on the frequency all night. Lucia had promised him supper and stayed too, writing what she heard on the back of a fuel chit. At first light another fishing boat found the Constancia safe, two miles north of where Hector had sent everyone. Lucia's chit had the right figures. Hector's had two digits swapped. By noon the harbormaster had telephoned to thank the field, and Amaro's small daughter had left a basket of bread at the gate. The coast station's log still carried Hector's position.

options.label: Correct the position in the coast station's log.
options.reply: The harbormaster's thanks become more careful, and the coast station learns which figures to ask for twice; Hector carries the page over himself.

options.label: Let the thanks stand and correct only Ines's ledger.
options.reply: The coast keeps its good story about the field, and the true position lives in green ink where only the four will think to look.

callback.text: Faria's brown tag hangs on a nail beside Hector's window. The stand went back on Friday; the loan now exists only because two men remember it.

condition_variants.trigger: has_capitulated = no has_war = no ac_sq_air_capable = yes
condition_variants.text: Ciro and Lucia were finishing a late training flight when Hector asked whether they had the fuel to look for a fishing boat. The Constancia had a dead engine and a southerly wind behind her, and the cloud sat low over the water. Lucia saw the lamp first, a small yellow point that kept vanishing in the swell. Ciro read the position from his kneeboard to Hector, who passed it to the coast station. On the ground Ciro found that he had written two digits the wrong way round. Lucia's own note was right. The lifeboat had found Amaro Reis and his crew anyway, after an hour searching the wrong water. By noon the harbormaster had telephoned his thanks, and Amaro's small daughter had left bread at the gate. The coast station's log still carried Ciro's figures.

chapters.title: Cause Unknown, Three Times
chapters.text: Ines found the pattern on a wet afternoon with the ledger open under the bench lamp. Three entries in two years: the same brake line union weeping after flights on the same aircraft, each marked cause unknown, each dry again before she reached it. She put the union on the bench and asked Ciro to hold the lamp. The seal inside carried fine bright file marks, the kind a careful person makes when he wants a part to seat without being replaced. Ciro knew the marks. He had made them after his own flights, unwilling to see the aircraft he had finally been trusted with grounded for a part the stores did not have. Lucia had known since spring and had promised to say nothing. Ines accused nobody. She turned the ledger toward him and waited.

options.label: Tell Ines whose file made those marks.
options.reply: Ines rewrites three causes in a single evening, and Lucia is hurt to find that a promise she kept for months is suddenly unnecessary.

options.label: Fit a new seal and leave the old causes unknown.
options.reply: The weeping stops tonight, and the ledger keeps its open question, a small blank Ines knows better than to fill in herself.

callback.text: Ciro once told Ines about a hangar door before she asked. It was easy then; it had cost him only a morning.

chapters.title: Lucia's Locker Door
chapters.text: Lucia kept her promises in grease pencil on the inside of her locker door and crossed them out as she kept them. By the morning of the open day the door held more than she could keep: a lift for Hector's father to the clinic on Thursdays, Ciro's weekend covered for his sister's wedding, the cooperative's boats hauled out before the storm. That last promise arrived at the gate on the shore road at eight. Anselmo Mendaro, the old harbor pilot, had brought a trailer and six fishermen and expected the field's tractor. The tractor was booked for the commander's display at eleven. Hector, who could smooth almost anything with a telephone, was already reaching for one. Ines asked Lucia, not unkindly, how many of the promises on that door had been hers to make.

options.label: Ask Hector to borrow the airport's tractor quietly.
options.reply: The boats come up the slip before the wind, the display runs on time, and Faria lends another favor Hector cannot write down.

options.label: Tell everyone at the gate who promised what.
options.reply: Anselmo laughs before the commander does; Lucia spends the open day apologizing in person, which costs her more than any tractor.

options.label: Haul the boats and let the display go without it.
options.reply: The commander's display is plainer than planned and he remembers who chose the fishermen; Lucia keeps one promise by breaking another in plain sight.

callback.text: Anselmo still tells the coast about the night the field helped bring the Constancia home. Hector smiles at the story and has never corrected the position.

chapters.title: Crates for the New System
chapters.text: The modernization began with crates. Three refurbished aircraft were promised from the north for the summer; first came a maintenance system with a terminal, a printer and a binder of codes. The two installers from Griswall were pleasant and in a hurry. They wanted the field's fault history entered before they left, and the system accepted a fault only as closed, with a code and a date. It had no field for why. Ines was asked to retire her ledger and offered, kindly, the job of entering codes. Ciro walked round the crates as if they might open from wanting. Lucia had promised the installers the history by Friday, and Hector kept them fed. Ines found that the comment line held sixty characters: enough for a cause, if nobody minded the field's improvisations traveling north with names attached.

options.label: Put the ledger's causes into the comment lines.
options.reply: The installers stay two extra days typing borrowed parts and filed seals sixty characters at a time, and Griswall receives the field's history with its names attached.

options.label: Keep the ledger on the bench beside the system.
options.reply: The new screen shows a clean history of closed faults, and the green ledger stays where the four can still read why.

callback.text: Three old faults are still marked cause unknown in Ines's hand. The new system will file them as closed unless somebody explains them first.

chapters.title: One Screen for Two Towers
chapters.text: The new approach radar was shared: its screen sat in the civil airport's tower across the runway, with a repeater in Hector's, and Hector and Dulce, the airport supervisor, had written the joint procedure over a long lunch. One bright afternoon Ciro was towing a refurbished aircraft across the shared runway when a light aircraft from the airport, already on short final, had to be sent around. Nothing touched and nobody was hurt. Hector's handover note had called the runway clear a minute before it was, and Dulce's controller had believed the note. Dulce came across the runway in person. She suggested they call it a learning conversation between friends rather than a report, and fix the wording themselves. Hector looked at the brown tag on its nail and thought about how much of the field rested on lunches.

options.label: Settle it over coffee between the two towers.
options.reply: The friendship between the towers survives the afternoon intact, and the procedure is corrected by two people who remember why it needed correcting.

options.label: File the joint report with both towers' notes.
options.reply: Dulce signs beside Hector without smiling, and both towers rewrite the handover in words a stranger on a night shift could follow.

callback.text: Faria's name has been in the station book since the stand was borrowed. Dulce knows it, and knows that the field writes things down.

chapters.title: The Stand with the Red Cloth
chapters.text: Ciro had scratched a panel while taxiing and wanted it smooth before morning. He worked alone after the shift, on the old maintenance stand Ines had tied a strip of red cloth around because one leg folded under weight. The panel was finished when the leg went. He landed on his left wrist and heard it break. Lucia found him an hour later, having promised to drive him home, and took him to the clinic; on the way they agreed he had slipped on hydraulic fluid by the door. In the morning the new commander asked for an accident account. The panel was perfect. The stand was back against the wall, and its red cloth lay on the floor where Ines found it. Ciro, in a cast to the elbow, looked at the cloth and then at Lucia.

options.label: Tell the commander about the stand and the night work.
options.reply: Ciro's flying restriction grows by a month and the stand is finally scrapped; Lucia has to take back a story she has already told twice.

options.label: Let the spilled fluid be the whole account.
options.reply: The accident form is tidy and nobody is reprimanded; Ines puts the red cloth in her drawer instead of in the ledger.

callback.text: Ciro once told Ines whose file had marked a seal. He knows exactly how much less that confession cost than this one will.

chapters.title: A Chair by the Tower Window
chapters.text: On bad nights Anselmo Mendaro walked to the field's gate on the shore road and asked for the harbor launch, which had been sold twenty years before. Hector had begun bringing his father up to the tower on night shifts. The old man sat by the window watching the water and was calm there, sometimes calling a current correctly before the coast station did. It broke every rule the field had. Lucia had promised the gate guards it was fine. Ines left a second cup of tea on the console, and Ciro drove the old man home at dawn. Then a new guard, who had been promised nothing, reported a civilian in the tower. The commander asked Hector to explain. Anselmo, who did not understand the question, offered the commander his chair.

options.label: Keep Anselmo's nights in the tower among the four.
options.reply: Lucia trades the new guard a promise of her own for his silence, and the old man keeps his chair by the window a while longer.

options.label: Ask openly for night shifts Hector can keep.
options.reply: Hector tells the commander more about his father than he has told his own sister, and the rota changes with everyone knowing why.

callback.text: Since the open day Lucia reads her promises aloud before she makes new ones. The one for Anselmo is written larger than the rest.

chapters.title: A Desk in Griswall
chapters.text: The offer had waited in Lucia's locker for three weeks: an instructor's post in Griswall, a housing allowance, and a school for her two boys that her husband Teo had already visited twice. She had decided to refuse it, and Teo had agreed after two long evenings. What remained was the commander's form, which asked for a reason. The true one would not fit the line. Ciro was flying again, and she had promised to fly beside him. Hector's father still needed his Thursdays. The field had too few people who knew which promises held it together, and she was one of them. Writing that would tell Griswall the field leaned on people it never listed. Writing family reasons would be shorter, and Teo would let it stand. Ines found her at the crew room table, pen still capped.

options.label: Write the true reason on the commander's form.
options.reply: The commander reads that the field depends on people it never lists, and Ciro hears from the commander, not from Lucia, what she gave up for him.

options.label: Write family reasons and keep the rest among us.
options.reply: Griswall is satisfied by a single line, and Ciro pretends not to know that the family had wanted to go.

callback.text: Anselmo still sits by the tower window on bad nights, and nobody has written it down. Lucia recognizes the same kind of question on this form.

chapters.title: Four Keels in the Cove
chapters.text: A spring gale drove four small boats from the south into the cove below the field. By dusk their crews had climbed the shore road to the gate, asking for water, a telephone and a dry floor. Two skippers had no papers for this coast. Lucia promised them the crew room and no questions before anyone asked what she was promising. Hector knew the coast station kept a list of every vessel sheltering on this shore, and that it trusted the field's lists. Joana Reis, the newest apprentice and Amaro's grown daughter, recognized one skipper from the harbor wall of her childhood and said nothing. Ines brought blankets from stores and wrote the number in her ledger without names. The gale would blow out by morning. The coast station's telephone sat on Hector's desk.

options.label: Give them the floor and keep no list.
options.reply: They sleep in the crew room under Lucia's promise, and at first light the cove is empty except for the marks of four keels in the sand.

options.label: Give the coast station every name and boat.
options.reply: Hector reads the names down the telephone slowly; one skipper leaves before dawn rather than hear his own name repeated.

callback.text: The coast station has trusted the field's figures since Hector corrected the Constancia position. He knows tonight will spend that trust one way or another.

condition_variants.text: The four boats in the cove below the field had come from the neighbor's coast, where the civil war had begun. They carried more than fishermen: a grandmother wrapped in a sail, two families with bedding, a skipper who said his town had changed hands twice and that he no longer knew whose list he would be on at home. They asked for water, a telephone and a floor, and they asked not to be written down. Lucia had already promised them the crew room. Hector had the coast station's request on his desk: every station on this shore was to report crossings. Joana Reis, the newest apprentice, whose father had once drifted toward that reef himself, carried the grandmother's bag up the road and asked her nothing. Ines brought blankets and wrote a number without names.

chapters.title: Lights without a Plan
chapters.text: The call came at two in the morning on the field's own frequency: a light cargo aircraft with no flight plan, lost in cloud, fuel nearly gone. Hector switched on the runway lights before he asked anybody's permission, and before he was sure who was asking for them. The aircraft landed long and stopped short of the fence. The pilot and his brother, who owned it, had flown without a proper reserve to save a contract; a report with their names would end the license and the small business together. Ciro, on duty, found a cracked oil cooler line and said nothing yet. Lucia made coffee for two frightened men. Ines opened her ledger to a clean page. Hector's own decision with the lights was the first thing any honest account of the night would have to contain.

options.label: Write the night down as it happened, names included.
options.reply: Hector's lights and the strangers' names go onto the same page, and Lucia must explain to frightened people why she poured them coffee first.

options.label: Write the night down and leave their names out.
options.reply: The account names Hector's decision and the cracked line but not the people, and Ines rules a line where the names would have gone.

options.label: Keep the night's account among the four.
options.reply: The page stays clean, the strangers keep their names, and Hector learns how easily a favor can be done for people he will never see again.

callback.text: The crews in the cove left no names behind them. Hector has wondered since whether he protected them, or only spared himself a telephone call.

condition_variants.text: The call came at two in the morning on the field's own frequency, in an accent from across the water: a transport from the neighbor's air arm, short of fuel, asking for any runway. Hector switched on the lights before he asked anybody's permission. The aircraft landed long and stopped short of the fence. Its crew would not say which side of their civil war had last given them orders, only that their families were in the back and that relatives at home would answer for any names that were printed. Ciro, on duty, found a cracked oil cooler line and said nothing yet. The commander was woken; Griswall would be told something. Ines opened her ledger to a clean page. Hector's own decision with the lights was the first thing any honest account would have to contain.

chapters.title: One Relay Short
chapters.text: The stores reconciliation came out one starter relay and one oil cooler line short. Joana Reis had done the count herself, her first, and had written missing, cause unknown in a careful hand. She brought the sheet to Ines to ask whether that was the right way to put it. Ciro, at the next bench, knew where both parts had gone: into the cargo aircraft that landed without a plan, fitted before dawn so it could leave before anyone with a clipboard arrived. Whatever else had been written about that night, nothing mentioned the parts. They were field property, and Ciro had paid for nothing. Ines looked at the count sheet, then at Ciro, and waited. Joana, who admired Ciro more than she had yet admitted to anyone, waited too.

options.label: Tell Joana and the stores office where the parts went.
options.reply: Joana corrects her count with a steadier hand than Ciro's, and the stores office sends a question north that Ciro must answer in person.

options.label: Rebuild them from the scrap bins and close the count.
options.reply: Ciro rebuilds a relay overnight from three dead ones, and Joana learns that some missing things are found by the people who lost them.

callback.text: Ines still keeps the red cloth from the old stand in her desk drawer. She does not take it out; Ciro knows exactly where it is.

condition_variants.text: The stores reconciliation came out one starter relay and one oil cooler line short. Joana Reis had done the count herself and written missing, cause unknown. Ciro knew where both parts had gone. When the transport from across the water was released, by an arrangement nobody at the field was shown, he had fitted them the night before so it would not fail over the sea. He had not asked which side of the neighbor's war would fly it next. No account of that landing mentioned the parts. Now a count sheet did, in an apprentice's careful hand. Writing the truth would put the field's stores, and Ciro's name, inside somebody else's civil war. Ines looked at the sheet, then at Ciro, and waited. Joana waited too.

chapters.title: Anselmo's Chart
chapters.text: Anselmo Mendaro was buried on a gray morning after a long illness, and the fishermen walked his coffin along the shore road past the field's gate. Afterward Hector brought his father's chart up to the crew room: forty years of soundings and currents in pencil, the best record of that coast anyone had. The coast station wanted it for their archive. In the margin by the reef was a note in Anselmo's younger hand, dated 1974: fog, a borrowed boat, a grounding he had let another skipper's crew take the blame for. The other skipper had been Joana's grandfather. The Reis family had never known. Joana was working in the hangar below, and had walked behind the coffin that morning. Ines read the note twice and offered no opinion. Hector rolled the chart and unrolled it again.

options.label: Show Joana the margin before the chart goes anywhere.
options.reply: Joana reads it twice and goes home to her father; the Reis family's condolences come a day later, quieter and more honest.

options.label: Keep the chart in the family, margin and all.
options.reply: The coast station receives a clean copy of the soundings, and Hector keeps his father's confession in a drawer of his own.

callback.text: The rota once changed because Hector told the commander about his father. Anselmo never knew how many people learned why his son worked days.

chapters.title: Every Volume
chapters.text: The inspectors from Griswall were reviewing the southern fields before the next budget, and they asked for the complete maintenance and incident history since 2000. The system could print its history in an afternoon: closed faults, codes, dates. Ines's ledgers filled most of a shelf. They held what the system did not: borrowed parts, filed seals, nights worked alone, the reasons behind the clean entries. Handed over, they might prove that the field did more with less than anyone in Griswall knew, or that it had been improvising beyond its rules for as long as Ines had kept them. Lucia had promised the inspectors everything at the gate before she knew what everything weighed. Ciro set the volumes on the crew room table without opening one. Hector asked which version of the field they meant to defend.

options.label: Give them the clean history and keep the ledgers.
options.reply: The inspectors leave with a tidy binder and a good opinion, and the shelf of green volumes stays where only the field can read it.

options.label: Give the inspectors every volume of the ledger.
options.reply: The inspectors stay a week instead of a day, and Ines answers for every improvisation with the people who made them sitting beside her.

callback.text: The green ledger has stood beside the system since the installers left. Until today nobody outside the field had asked which one was the record.

condition_variants.text: The inspectors from Griswall asked for the complete history since 2000, and since the neighbor's civil war began they wanted the crossing years as well: every unscheduled landing, every boat that sheltered in the cove, every part issued to anybody who was not Aurelian. The system could print closed faults in an afternoon. Ines's ledgers filled most of a shelf and held what the system did not: borrowed parts, filed seals, nights worked alone, numbers of people without their names. Some of those people still had relatives across the water. Handed over, the ledgers might show a field that did more with less, or one that had made its own policy on a coast where policy was meant to come from Griswall. Lucia had promised the inspectors everything at the gate. Ciro set the volumes on the crew room table.

chapters.title: The Old Set Comes Down
chapters.text: The weak coast set was coming down at last, replaced by a combined system shared with the coast station and the civil airport. On its final evening Faria, long retired, came across the runway to listen to it with Hector. The handover form had a section headed standing agreements. Hector's real agreements were in a notebook in his shirt pocket: which skipper would relay for whom, which favors the airport workshop owed and was owed, which telephone numbers answered at night. The new controller was young, careful and from the north. Without the notebook she would have to earn the coast's trust from nothing. Written into the handover, every quiet arrangement would become something somebody could audit or forbid. Faria's brown tag still hung on its nail. Hector turned the old set's volume up one last time.

options.label: Write the standing arrangements into the handover.
options.reply: The new controller receives a map of favors she can use and question, and two old skippers stop answering Hector's telephone for a month.

options.label: Hand over the procedures and keep the notebook.
options.reply: The handover is clean and the notebook goes home in Hector's pocket; the new controller will earn the coast one telephone call at a time.

callback.text: Dulce's signature still sits beside Hector's on the old joint report. She telephones to ask whether the new system will remember why that handover wording changed.

chapters.title: The Readiness Return
chapters.text: The autumn readiness return asked one plain question: how many of the field's aircraft could fly tomorrow. The commander wanted five. Ines's ledger supported two without qualification and three more only because of parts kept in repair well past their limits, most of them by Ciro, some in ways no manual described. Joana, qualified now and trusted with the return, laid both numbers side by side on the bench under the lamp. Ciro said the three would fly; he had flown them. Ines said that was a reason, not a number. Lucia had promised the commander the return by noon, and Hector had heard from the airport that Griswall was comparing fields. Joana looked at the pencil, then at the four people who had taught her that a count could be honest or kind.

options.label: Write the number the ledger supports.
options.reply: Joana writes two and signs it, the commander's displeasure lands on all five of them, and the field is measured by what it can actually do.

options.label: Write the commander's number; keep the reasons in the ledger.
options.reply: The return reaches Griswall complete and on time, and three qualified aircraft stay serviceable on paper and in Ciro's hands.

callback.text: Ciro once rebuilt a relay from three dead ones so a count could close. Joana remembers, and asks which numbers on this page were made the same way.

Ciro said the three would fly and that he would take the worst of them himself. Ines said that was a reason, not a number. Hector was on the telephone to the coast station, which wanted to know what the field could cover.

chapters.title: Beds for the Northern Crews
chapters.text: The northern crews arrived at the gate on the shore road in two buses, sent south while their own field was closed for work nobody had explained to this one. Forty people came with their tool chests and their records in cardboard boxes. Lucia had promised them beds before she counted the beds. There were twenty-six. Ines had counted the stores too, and the field's thinness showed in every figure: parts borrowed, parts rebuilt, aircraft listed that flew on Ciro's patience. The visiting crew chief wanted to know what she was walking into. Hector had already telephoned the civil airport about its empty hangar and Faria's successor about spare cots. It would be easy to make room first and let the field's real condition come out later, one awkward discovery at a time.

options.label: Tell the newcomers what the field can really give.
options.reply: The crew chiefs hear about borrowed parts and rebuilt relays before they unpack, and Lucia watches her promise of beds become an honest shortage.

options.label: Make room first and explain the field later.
options.reply: Everyone sleeps somewhere by midnight, and the newcomers learn the field's real condition one awkward discovery at a time.

callback.text: The commander's form once recorded that the field leaned on people it never listed. Lucia is about to promise beds to more of them.

chapters.capitulated_text: The country had capitulated, and the northern crews came to the gate on the shore road because the order that sent them south had never been canceled by anybody still able to cancel it. Forty people arrived with tool chests and records in cardboard boxes. An officer of the new administration had taken a desk in the commander's office two days earlier, polite and tired, asking for lists. Lucia had promised the newcomers beds before she counted them. There were twenty-six. Ines's stores showed the field's thinness in every figure: parts borrowed, parts rebuilt, aircraft that had flown on Ciro's patience and were not flying now. The visiting crew chief wanted to know what she was walking into, and what to say when the officer asked. Hector had the civil airport on the telephone, asking the same.

condition_variants.text: Griswall was held from across the water, and the southern field had become one of the few places where Aurelian crews could still report for work. They came to the gate on the shore road in whatever would carry them: buses, a bakery van, a tractor Faria's successor had lent without asking anyone. Their records had stayed in the north. Lucia had promised beds before she counted them. There were twenty-six beds and more than a hundred people. Ines's ledger was suddenly the only maintenance history anyone here could consult, and it described a field held together by borrowing and patience. The northern crew chiefs wanted to know what they were walking into. Hector was already on the telephone to the civil airport about its empty terminal. Making room first would be easy; the truth could wait.

condition_variants.text: The war with Leasath had come across the water, and within days the shore road was full. Crews from fields that could no longer work arrived at the gate in buses and borrowed vans, with tool chests, children and records in cardboard boxes. Lucia had promised them beds before she counted them. There were twenty-six. Ines's stores showed the field's thinness in every figure: parts borrowed, parts rebuilt, aircraft listed that flew on Ciro's patience. The newcomers' crew chiefs wanted to know what they were walking into and what the field could really keep serviceable. Hector had the civil airport on one telephone and the coast station on the other. Nobody at the gate was asking for an inspection, only for somewhere to sleep. Making room first would be easy. The truth would come out one discovery at a time.

The declaration everyone on the coast had been waiting for was withheld. The government across the water had chosen, for its own reasons, not to send it, and the radio said so in a sentence that sounded unfinished. The northern crews sent south as a precaution arrived at the gate on the shore road anyway, two buses of them, with tool chests and records in cardboard boxes and nobody to tell them whether to unpack. Lucia had promised beds before she counted them. There were twenty-six. Ines's stores showed the field's thinness in every figure: parts borrowed, parts rebuilt, aircraft listed that flew on Ciro's patience. Relief made everyone generous and nobody curious. Hector arranged cots with the civil airport. The visiting crew chief asked what kind of field she had come to.

The northern crews came south anyway, sent to watch the cove and the boats that still crossed it at night. Two buses stopped at the gate on the shore road with tool chests and records in cardboard boxes. Lucia had promised beds before she counted them. There were twenty-six. chapters.title: Ciro's Tin
chapters.text: Joana asked Ciro to teach her the repairs that were not in any manual. She had watched them for eleven years: the shim cut from a drinks can, the seal reseated with a jeweler's file, the relay rebuilt from three dead ones. They lived in a dented biscuit tin in his locker, and in his hands. One evening he set the tin on the crew room table and opened it, and the four of them looked at thirty years of private work. Some of those repairs had kept aircraft flying that should have been grounded. Some had been better than the proper parts. Ines had written down the ones she knew about; Lucia knew several Ines did not. Written into the field's procedures, they would outlive him, and so would the record of every limit he had stretched.

options.label: Teach them by hand and keep the tin.
options.reply: Joana learns the repairs at the bench with Ciro's hands over hers, and the methods survive exactly as long as the people who trust each other.

options.label: Write every repair into the procedures, limits included.
options.reply: Ciro spends three evenings dictating to Joana, and the pages record both what worked and every limit he stretched to make it work.

callback.text: Joana corrected her count once because Ciro told her plainly where the parts had gone. She expects the same plainness from him now.

chapters.capitulated_text: The country had capitulated, the field's aircraft stood idle under the new administration, and the officer in the commander's office had asked for an inventory of tools. Joana asked Ciro whether the repairs that were not in any manual would simply be lost now. He set his dented biscuit tin on the crew room table and opened it: the shim cut from a drinks can, the seal reseated with a jeweler's file, the relay rebuilt from three dead ones. Thirty years of private work, none of it on any list the officer held. Written into the field's procedures, the methods would outlive the four of them and whatever administration came next, in a file anyone could read. Taught by hand, they would survive only in the people Ciro trusted. Lucia closed the door.

condition_variants.text: Griswall was Aurelian again, and the crews who had come south were packing for the road north, their tool chests full of parts kept in service here by every means the field possessed. Before they left, Joana asked Ciro to put the repairs that were not in any manual where the departing crews could see them. He set his dented biscuit tin on the crew room table and opened it: the shim cut from a drinks can, the seal reseated with a jeweler's file, the relay rebuilt from three dead ones. Some of those repairs were now inside machines that would go north with people who had never met him. Ines had written down the ones she knew; Lucia knew several more. The northern crews would inherit the repairs either way. The question was whether they would inherit the record.

Since the war with the neighbor began, the field had been crowded with crews from the north, and the stores had emptied faster than any ledger could follow. One evening Joana asked Ciro to teach the newcomers the repairs that were not in any manual. He set his dented biscuit tin on the crew room table and opened it: the shim cut from a drinks can, the seal reseated with a jeweler's file, the relay rebuilt from three dead ones. Thirty years of private work lay between the four of them and a dozen strangers who needed it now. Some of those repairs had kept aircraft serviceable that should have been grounded. Ines had written down the ones she knew; Lucia knew several Ines did not. Ciro would rather teach them by hand.

chapters.title: Kept in Repair
chapters.text: Ines closed the ninth volume of her ledger on the last working day of the year, with one page left blank for whoever came next. She had decided to stop being the only person who kept it. The question was where it would go. Joana wanted it on the bench, where it had always been. The field's archive wanted all nine volumes, catalogued and open to anyone with a reason to ask, which would include people none of them had met. Ciro had brought the hangar door's old wheel, replaced that week after thirty years of being kept in repair. Lucia had wiped her locker door clean except for one line. Hector had taken Faria's brown tag off its nail and set it on the table. The four of them sat with the volumes between them and waited for Ines.

options.label: Leave the ledgers open to whoever keeps the field next.
options.reply: Ines writes an index for strangers, and the four accept that people they will never meet may judge every repair the volumes describe.

options.label: Give the ledgers to Joana to keep as Ines kept them.
options.reply: Joana carries the nine volumes to the bench, and the field's real history stays in the hands of people who already know how to read it.

callback.text: Joana read Anselmo's margin before the chart went anywhere. She knows better than anyone what it costs a family when an old account is finally written down.

chapters.capitulated_text: The country had capitulated, and the officer in the commander's office had asked, politely, for the field's maintenance records before the end of the year. The system's history had already been printed for him. On the last working day Ines closed the ninth volume of her ledger with one page left blank and set all nine on the crew room table. The volumes held thirty years of borrowed parts and stretched limits, and the numbers, sometimes the names, of people who had crossed the water or sheltered in the cove. Left open in the field's archive, they would belong to whoever kept the field next. Given to Joana, they would stay among people who understood them, outside any account the new administration could read. Hector set Faria's brown tag on the table. Ciro waited for Ines.

Ines closed the ninth volume of her ledger with one page left blank. The war months filled most of it: parts borrowed from the civil airport, aircraft kept serviceable past every limit, northern crews' names beside repairs made on a field not their own. She had decided to stop being the only person who kept it. Joana wanted it on the bench. The field's archive wanted all nine volumes, open to anyone with a reason to ask, including strangers who would one day judge these months from outside them. Hector set Faria's brown tag on the table. The four of them waited for Ines.

Griswall was Aurelian again, and most of the northern crews had gone home by the last working day of the year, leaving cots folded in the civil airport's hangar and notes of thanks in Lucia's locker. Ines closed the ninth volume of her ledger with one page left blank. Its last months held the capital's occupation as the field had lived it: borrowed parts, stretched limits, strangers' names beside repairs made on a field not their own. The reopening offices in Griswall wanted the southern fields' histories. The field's own archive wanted all nine volumes, open to anyone with a reason to ask. Joana wanted them on the bench. Ciro had brought the hangar door's old wheel, replaced at last. Hector set Faria's brown tag on the table. The four of them waited for Ines.

Ines closed the ninth volume of her ledger with one page left blank. She had decided to stop being the only person who kept it. Relief had made the whole coast generous, and generosity made it easy to put old things away without reading them. The field's archive wanted all nine volumes, open to anyone with a reason to ask. endings.title: The Page Left Blank
endings.text: Joana makes the first entry in the tenth volume while the four are still in the room, and nobody corrects her. Ciro's repairs are in it with his name and their limits; he no longer mends things before anyone sees, but where Joana can watch and argue. Lucia's locker door carries one promise at a time now, and she says no out loud, which she still finds harder than flying. Hector returns Faria's tag to the airport workshop, where somebody laughs and pins it to their board beside a new loan written down in ink. Ines no longer keeps the ledger alone. She reads it with whoever asks, and is surprised how rarely the truth in it hurts the people it names. They have not become people who never break things. They have become people who say what broke, and stay in the room while it is mended.

endings.title: Kept Among Four
endings.text: The field works, and anyone can see that it works. The system's history is clean, the procedures are current, and visitors leave with a good opinion. The green ledgers sit in a locked cabinet in the crew room, and only four people, and perhaps Joana, know what they hold. Ciro still mends things before anyone sees, more skillfully than ever. Lucia keeps most of her promises and carries the rest privately, as she always has. Hector's arrangements with the coast and the airport survive because he does, and he has begun to wonder what happens when he does not. Ines trusts the other three completely and has stopped expecting anyone else to read what she writes. Their friendship has protected each of them for thirty years. It has not taught the field how to know itself without the four of them in it.

endings.title: Parts Returned Separately
endings.text: There is no single quarrel to point to, only thirty years of accounts that each of them kept a little differently. Ines gives the ledgers to the archive and walks home alone, relieved and unaccountably angry. Ciro leaves his biscuit tin on the bench without a note, which Joana takes as a gift and the others as a reproach. Lucia wipes her locker door clean and promises nobody anything on the way out, which frightens her more than she admits. Hector hangs Faria's tag back on its nail for the new controller and does not explain it. All four are alive and well, and still capable of the decency that kept the field working. They have simply stopped believing that what one of them keeps private and what another writes down can belong to the same story. They leave the hangar by different doors.
